newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo stocks recover from steep drop, Hong Kong quiet.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks recover from steep drop, Hong Kong quiet.

text.p: Tokyo stocks were buffeted in another volatile session on Tuesday, falling sharply before rebounding.
Hong Kong's market, however, was subdued ahead of the release of key U.S. inflation data later in the day.
Other Asian markets were generally mixed. Seoul shares topped the list of winners with a gain of more than 4 percent.
Tokyo traders said the Japanese market's rebound could mark the end of frenzied selling -- at least for now.

Brokers said last-minute buying of blue chips rescued the Nikkei average from its loss of over 500 points in early trading. The benchmark average of 225 leading shares closed 25.66 points, or 0.14 percent, lower at 18,093.13.
Despite the rebound, many brokers warned that perils of a resumed tumble remain.
"What the government needs to do is to take swift action to realise structural reforms in the economy," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.
Hong Kong stocks closed slightly higher ahead of the U.S. inflation report. The Hang Seng Index scraped out a 4.66-point advance to close at 13,293.87.

"If this CPI (consumer price index) report turns out to be a non-event, I think we will see both the U.S. and Hong Kong markets move up again," said Charles Cheung, executive director at J&A Securities.
South Korean stocks closed sharply higher after a weak response to all-out strike calls and increasing fund inflows boosted sentiment, brokers said.
Blue-chip manufacturing stocks, which stood to be major casualties from the strikes, soared to close at daily limits.
The composite index climbed 4.1 percent, or 27.05 points, to a provisional close at 686.59.

Thai stocks finished 1.85 percent lower amid worries over whether banks would get involved in a government plan to help troubled property developers, brokers said. The SET index fell 15.22 points to 807.67.
The Bombay 30-share index rallied for the sixth consecutive session to end 34.28 points, or 0.99 percent, higher at a provisional close of 3,487.44.
In Singapore, the benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index ended at 2,215.52, down 16.88 points.

A fall in Kuala Lumpur stocks was sparked by a lack of foreign institutional buyers, profit taking and concerns over the weak Tokyo bourse, traders said. The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks fell 9.34 points to 1,211.04.
"We have been strong in the last two weeks. I think today is profit taking and forced selling," said one research chief.

Taiwan shares saw their strong opening evaporate as a surge through six-year resistance at 7,200 sparked profit-taking from a recent five percent rally. The index lost 51.71 points or 0.72 percent to end at 7,137.76, off a midsession high of 7,246.66.

Manila stocks paused for a respite, closing slightly lower after a seven-day run as players sold blue-chip issues. The main index ended down 8.59 points, or 0.26 percent, at 3,261.72. Australian shares ended a listless session marginally lower as traders found little inspiration locally or elsewhere. The All Ordinaries index shed 2.9 points to 2,419.4.
February Brent was last traded at $23.40 per barrel, down eight cents from London, while March shed nine cents to $23.05.
Hong Kong gold bullion ended at US$356.80/357.30 an ounce against New York's US$358.30/70 close on Monday.

The dollar was clawing ts way back up again against the yen in late Tokyo after falling earlier on remarks by the Toyota Motor president that an appropriate dollar/yen level would be 100-110 yen. At 1101 GMT, the dollar traded at 116.43/48 yen and 1.5881/88 marks.
